sections.heading: 2. The one thing that would unblock everything — a single supervised launch

blocks.html: One launch. Not a session of launches. Nothing on this page has ever been seen running — every visual claim here is offline arithmetic from the C++, the shaders and the shipped mission data. That is real evidence and it caught real bugs, but it cannot tell you whether a thing looks right. A single supervised launch would close the largest open set on this page at once: whether any of the nine default-ON changes look right, whether the cursor fix holds, and the popup-turret question that no amount of source reading can settle.

The open question worth answering plainly

The SH-IBL probe that lights every static prop is never rotated to the mission sun. It is baked once with a fixed bright axis, and on 17 of the 24 missions that leaves a building brighter on the wall facing away from the sun. The median aim error is 106°; the worst, mc2_14, is 177° — almost exactly backwards. I re-derived this from the shipped coefficient table rather than trusting the harness, and got 17 of 24 independently. The fix is written and landed (f16b49e96) but gated OFF, because nobody has ever seen it render — and, as the table above says, it is not in any binary you can launch. The question for you: is a defect that is live on every default launch today worth a rebuild to look at?

Shoreline: DISPLACEMENT, FACETING, or the third thing?
still a one-word answer — but the question has changed since it was first written

Look at the mc2_17 waterline and say which you are seeing. (a) DISPLACEMENT — the edge is in the wrong place, cutting across land or sea. (b) FACETING — the edge is in the right place but built from visible straight risers instead of a curve. (c) A GLOW TRACING THE TILE GRID — the edge itself is fine, but something bright is drawn along it in steps, worst at night.
You can answer (a) vs (b) from the two plots in §20a without launching anything: they draw the stock waterline against the 128 wu tile lattice for both maps. On mc2_17 the stock line is a smooth sinuous curve that crosses tile boundaries freely; on mc2_10 it is a right-angle staircase locked to the lattice. If what you see on mc2_17 looks like the mc2_10 plot, that is displacement and the offline data is wrong about the map. Caveat stated plainly: those are offline contour plots of the shipping heightfield, not rendered frames — no rendered engine frame of mc2_17 water exists anywhere on disk.

Two corrections since this row was written, and the second one is a live lead.
(1) The arithmetic that used to appear here is withdrawn. This row previously said “the arithmetic says (b): a 128 wu tile projects to ~147 px at the intro camera and you measured risers of 138–148 px”. That px pair has no derivation anywhere in the repo — no script, no measurement JSON, no status doc — and an identical “137–148px” string does exist, in tools/visual_verify/regions/mc2_10_saved_204523.json, describing mc2_10 at a top-down pose. It was most likely re-attributed to mc2_17. A number that may belong to the other map must not be allowed to pick your answer, so it has been removed rather than repeated.
(2) A default-ON candidate cause that all six shoreline lanes missed. MC2_TERRAIN_SHORELINE has three readers and they disagree: gos_terrain_lod_chunk.cpp:2659 and mclib/terrain.cpp:1120 both read !(v && v[0]=='0') → default ON, while gos_TerrainLodChunk_IsShorelineMaskActive() at gos_terrain_lod_chunk.cpp:3903 reads (v && v[0] && v[0]!='0') → default OFF. That third reader is the one that suppresses the legacy screen-space runShoreline() pass (gos_postprocess.cpp:3404). Because it is false on an unset environment, the suppression never fires and the legacy glow runs on every stock frame with water, alongside the V3 band it was supposed to replace. The engine’s own comment at :2659 says that legacy pass “traced the raw tile-quantized water-mesh edge and amplified the staircase at night”. Chain re-verified end to end for this page. If your answer is (c), that is where the fix is, and it is a one-line change.

5.1  The cursor-capture fix — ffebf5e87

What it means for you: an offscreen run should now be unable to touch your mouse, your keyboard or your foreground window. That was the failure that cost you this session — MC2_WINDOW_OFFSCREEN=1 parked the window at (-32000,-32000), then showed it, and Win32 ClipCursor confined your physical pointer to a rectangle on no monitor. The offscreen mode that existed to keep agent runs off your desktop was itself taking your cursor, and the focus-gained handler re-armed the grab after any startup-only suppression.

Geometry failsafe, independent of every environment variable: ClipCursor is refused outright when the rectangle lands on no monitor, so you can always reach your own desktop
No taskbar button, no Alt-Tab entry, no foreground activation on an unattended run — applied before the window is ever mapped

5.2  Launch isolation — none of the mechanisms proved safe, the block stays

.claude/LAUNCH-ISOLATION-VALIDATION.md (c09234f6f, 446 lines) assessed every candidate mechanism for letting an agent launch the game without touching your desktop. None was proven safe. This is the evidence behind decision 11 in the queue above, and it is the reason section 2 asks you rather than proposing a workaround.

REFUTED — measured absent or actively disruptive

NOT REFUTED — and NOT PROVEN. The only candidate still standing, and the one measurement that would settle it was deliberately not taken: a scheduled task is persistent machine configuration, which is your decision and not an agent’s.

blocks.html: The escape was reproduced, in four unprivileged calls. A process confined to a private window station walked straight back out to your interactive desktop with OpenWindowStationW("WinSta0") → SetProcessWindowStation → OpenDesktopW("Default") → SetThreadDesktop. Same user, same token, no administrator rights. The earlier lane’s proof of the opposite turned out to be a tautology — it called OpenDesktopW from inside the private station, where desktop names resolve relative to the caller’s own station, so that call was guaranteed to fail and tested nothing. The call that decides it had never been made.

Two limits the study states about its own evidence, and they matter. (1) The engine was never launched — not once, in any lane; every measurement came from throwaway probe processes. (2) Every run happened with the workstation locked, so every “the supervisor saw no change to foreground or cursor” result is a null instrument: it was comparing nothing to nothing. That evidence carries no information and must not be read as reassurance. The study’s own recommendation was to fix the offscreen cursor defect independently of the isolation question — “it removes a live trap, and it does not lift or weaken the block in any way” — which is what 5.1 did, 37 minutes later.
5.3  The burial audit — and why the world will look like it shifted

scripts/object_burial_audit.py (6d9360046) is a line-by-line offline port of MapData::terrainElevation(). It answers, without launching anything, which elevation function the shipped mission data was actually authored on — across all 72,153 stock objects on all 37 shipped maps, with zero unresolved rows. I re-ran it in full today; the numbers below are from that run, not quoted.

blocks.html: Read it like this. The authored height of every object matches the Phong-retired heightfield to within 0.0001 world units on every class, and disagrees with the legacy CPU-Phong heightfield by up to 13.39 wu (2.67 m). The shipped data was authored on the plain triangle-linear heightfield. That independently validates the CPU Phong retirement (a75339bb0, default-ON) — it was not a taste call, and the engine had been grounding objects on an elevation the map authors never used.

⚠ CARRY THIS WARNING INTO YOUR FIRST LAUNCH. Relative to the build immediately before it, 56,395 objects change their apparent burial — 78% of all 72,153 placed objects, and 91% of the non-re-snapping ones. They move in both directions: 27,439 settle down (they had been floating) and 28,956 rise up (they had been sunk), by up to ±11.84 world units — about ±2.4 metres (worldUnitsPerMeter = 5.01, mclib/terrain.cpp:103). The movers are overwhelmingly trees. Your first launch will look like the world shifted vertically. That is correct, and it will still be startling. The audit tool says why in its own output: in both directions the post-retire value is exactly the geometric burial, because the authored height equals the plain ground for every object — the move is a correction, not a new error, but it IS user-visible relative to the immediately preceding build. If it looks wrong to you, MC2_CPU_PHONG_RETIRE=0 is the single complete revert.

Reproduce it yourself: py -3 scripts/object_burial_audit.py --top 0 for the table, --selftest for its eight negative controls (I ran them today: ALL PASS, including a mutation control that re-parses with the wrong byte layout and requires it to be rejected, and an axis control that requires the wrong up-axis to give a visibly different answer). One caveat worth knowing: the script needs stock mission data it finds in a sibling install, not in the worktree, and it byte-verifies whatever it finds against the shipped mission.fst and refuses data it cannot verify. A clone alone is not enough — an install has to be present.

blocks.html: Everything here was published to you or relayed to you, and is now withdrawn or restated. Each was re-checked against the source tree for this update; where a number could not be found in the repo at all it is withdrawn rather than repeated with a hedge. rows.html: “The mc2_17 waterline arithmetic proves FACETING — a 128 wu tile projects to ~147 px and you measured risers of 138–148 px.”

Withdrawn. That pair has no derivation anywhere in the repo. A near-identical string does exist — tools/visual_verify/regions/mc2_10_saved_204523.json — but it describes mc2_10 at a near-top-down pose, a different map and a different camera. A number that may belong to mc2_10 must not pick your answer about mc2_17. Decision 1 below still needs your one-word answer; it just no longer comes with a thumb on the scale.
“The legacy shoreline pass glows the water edge.”

It cannot touch a water pixel. A census of every fragment shader writing attachment 1: the pass selects on alpha in (0.15, 0.35); both water shaders write 0.0, chunk terrain writes 1.0, the buffer clear is 0.0. The only producers in band are static_prop.frag at 0.25 and 0.1875. So it has been applying an animated foam brighten to static-prop pixels near terrain — a shimmer on building and fence silhouettes. One qualifier the relay dropped: this holds on the default terrain stack. Under MC2_TERRAIN_LOD_CHUNK=0 the legacy terrain shader does land in the band and the pass does foam water.
“…therefore the mc2_17 staircase must be terrain-side or water-mesh-side, and the three dead cures were aimed correctly.”

Not supported — I was asked to publish this and it does not hold. The census rules out one candidate; it does not narrow the rest. Terrain LOD decimation is explicitly recorded as an open, untested rival. And the three cures were not aimed correctly: mc2_17’s waterline measures a staircase index of 0.260 against a 0.222 floor for a smooth curve — it is barely stair-stepped at all — while mc2_10 measures 0.737. All three cures were verified on mc2_10 and mc2_01, never on mc2_17. No rendered engine frame of mc2_17 water exists anywhere on disk, which is why decision 1 is still yours.

Inverted — at night it is a lift. On mc2_10 (a night mission) the vehicle ambient floor takes 97%+ of vehicle vertices 0.753 → 1.0, a 1.33× lift. The precision that makes this fair: the same 1.33 exists with the opposite sign eight hours earlier the same day — VEHICLE-LIGHTING-PATH-1 alone took shadow faces 1.0 → 0.753, and VEHICLE-AMBIENT-FLOOR-1 put it back. So “darker at night” was a true description of a build that existed for eight hours. It is not true of what you have. The real documented darkening is a daylight event on mc2_03.
“Trees are the darkest asset class at every shipped colour scheme, and mechs are the brightest — a rank that flips on 5 of 10 schemes.”

Half of this is withdrawn. Tree median albedo L = 58.0 is real. But “darkest class” is contradicted inside the same document, which elsewhere lists unpainted mech 47.0 and vehicle 48.4 below it. And “at every colour scheme” is not a property trees can have — trees are never repainted, so their number is scheme-independent by construction. The “5 of 10” is withdrawn entirely: no such sweep output exists on disk, and “10” is a tool’s default --paint-sweep-limit, not a count of shipped schemes. What survives, and is well sourced: the paint scheme moves brightness further than any lighting effect under study (mech 71.2–117.2, a 1.65× range), so “which asset class is brightest” is not a stable question.

“Sunk turrets: the 11 turret-class objects sit on the heightfield to 2e-6 wu, but three L_TurretGenerator objects have 47.95% of their mesh below their origin — and the black-quad report names the same two models.”

Only the first number survives, and the last clause is wrong. There are exactly 11 TURRET-class objects on mc2_03 — confirmed from the mission object list. But “2e-6” and “47.95%” appear nowhere in the repo; the decisive offline check (placed z vs terrain elevation) is specified and has never been run, and the mission .pak is not in this worktree. The black-quad report names BTurretControl and LiaoTurretGenerator — two model types, only one of which overlaps, so “the same two models” cannot be true of a three-instance single-model group. See the question below.

“Roughly half the props in the world move vertically by up to ±2.4 m.”
relayed for publication — and then wrongly withdrawn on this page

The ±2.4 m half is RIGHT — this page withdrew it yesterday and the withdrawal was wrong. The fleet-wide maximum is ±11.8379 world units, and the engine’s own conversion is stated outright on two adjacent engine lines — float worldUnitsPerMeter = 5.01f; and float metersPerWorldUnit = 0.2f; (mclib/terrain.cpp:103-104), neither ever reassigned, direction confirmed at code/controlgui.cpp:645. 11.8379 wu = 2.36 m, which rounds to the 2.4 you were given. What is genuinely understated is “roughly half”: the measured figure is 78% of all 72,153 objects — 96.5% of trees, and 48.8–63.6% of every non-tree class, so “roughly half” describes the non-tree population and understates the whole. Why the bad withdrawal is left on the page instead of quietly deleted: I searched the audit script for a metre conversion, did not find one, and concluded the unit was invented — but the conversion lives in the engine, which I had not opened. I then found a 2.479 in a percentile of a small subsample and published it as the figure’s origin. That was a digit coincidence, not a derivation (2.479 wu is 0.49 m). It is the exact mistake this page keeps warning about, made by the page itself.

“MC2_STATIC_PROP_IBL_SUN_ROTATE is absent from all three binaries and cannot be graded by you at all.”
published in section 1 of this page

Out of date, not wrong. It was true of the three installs that existed when it was written. The strongest finding of the session is gradable. It still has never been looked at.
“The rank flips on 5 of 10 schemes, so ‘mechs are the brightest’ is not robust.”

Withdrawn. The 10 is a command-line default (--paint-sweep-limit) that merely caps how many schemes get iterated — a flag default wearing a measurement’s clothes. The real population is 114 mission-authored schemes, and no reading reproduces 5-of-10. The qualitative claim survives: paint scheme swings mech albedo 1.58× over 10 schemes and 5.66× over all 114, so “mechs are the brightest” is not a scheme-stable property. Say that; do not say 5 of 10.

“Trees are the darkest asset class at every shipped colour scheme.”
this page previously withdrew the whole claim; that went too far

Restated, and the restated form is true. Trees are the darkest as-drawn class (median L 58.0, against vehicle 96.9, static prop 103.9, mech 112.0) — and trivially so at every scheme, because trees are never repainted: paint applies only to mech and vehicle. “At every scheme” is not a property trees can have. The trap: at the raw texture convention — a paint mask that is never drawn — mech reads 47.0 and vehicle 48.4, below tree, and you conclude the opposite. Always say as-drawn.

“The turret arithmetic (2e-6 wu, 47.95%) appears nowhere in the repo — the decisive check has never been run.”
an objection this page relied on

The objection was reasonable when written and is now false. The check had been run twice; it has since been run a third time, and the entire apparatus — the 1,314-line tool and both result tables — is committed at 6d9360046. It was untracked, not absent. This is the session’s most expensive recurring mistake in miniature: a lane measures a number, reports it, and never commits the artifact; the next lane greps the repo, finds nothing, and grades it fabricated. Both behaved correctly. The repo is not a record of what was measured — it is a record of what was committed.

“47.95% of the L_TurretGenerator mesh is below its origin.”
quoted bare

The number is right; the impression it creates is wrong. The −24.93 comes entirely from an 8-vertex decorative Coil card that straddles the origin symmetrically. The actual body is 1.22% below origin. Anyone quoting 47.95% is describing a decoration, not a sunk building. Quote 1.22%, or quote both. Also: that prop is BUILDING-class and re-snaps to ground every frame, so the authored-height columns do not even apply to it.

blocks.html: A question only you can answer: which thing is “sunk”?

Your report said turrets are sunk. Two different populations answer to that word and they have different cures, so the wrong guess costs a lane. (a) The 11 TURRET-class objects — real turrets, which never re-snap their height after placement, and which the CPU-Phong retire above is a direct candidate explanation for. (b) The turret-named but building-class props, i.e. LiaoTurretGenerator and BTurretControl — the same two models named in the separate black-quad defect, which re-snap every frame and behave differently. And one more thing worth a word: are they sunk from the moment the mission loads, or only after they turn or fire? That single distinction separates a placement bug from an animation bug and nobody can infer it from source.

Where these come from. Every correction above is adjudicated in .claude/MEASUREMENT-LEDGER.md, which grades each disputed number three ways — measured and reproducible, measured but uncommitted, or unsupported. The middle category is the point of the file: “I could not find it in the repo” is evidence of non-commitment, not of falsity. Nothing graded unsupported appears anywhere on this page.

blocks.html: User report (mc2_10 night): a building's light-facing parts are FULLY lit and its away-facing parts dark, but nothing accounts for occlusion by the building's own geometry — a wall behind a taller wing, a recessed courtyard, an inset doorway or the underside of an overhang all render full-bright.

blocks.html: NO CODE CHANGE WAS NEEDED — and none was made. Both mechanisms were already shipped and simply switched off. Root cause is three stacked things: (1) static_prop.frag writes the a=0.25 "no self shadow" GBuffer class and shadow_screen.frag deliberately skips the dynamic cascade for it ("CPU never self-shadowed buildings"); (2) the baked base light is a per-LEAF constant (GetARGBHighlight(), one scalar per TG_Shape), so it adds no intra-surface variation, and calc_light has no occlusion term at all; (3) what is left is a pure per-face max(N·L,0) — precisely "fully lit or dark, nothing between". Props already cast into the CSM cascades, so no caster-set widening was required and the alpha-card foliage exclusion was never touched.

Why BOTH gates. MC2_PROP_SHADOW_RECEIVE opts props back into the dynamic cascade — that gives coarse wing-on-wing shadow, but the cascades are map-sized and cannot resolve a doorway reveal. MC2_SSAO adds the fine contact term (recesses, inside corners, undersides) using depth + GBuffer normals props already write. Measured on mc2_01 day: RECEIVE alone changes 0.25-0.73% of pixels and 100% of them get DARKER, zero brighter (a pure occlusion term can only darken — animation or a lighting bug could not be one-sided); adding SSAO multiplies coverage 20-60x (to 1.5-14.7%) while staying ~99% darker.

Night compound walls + domes — OFF (top) vs RECEIVE only (bottom): dome flanks, the crevice between adjacent domes, and buttress slopes darken.

At mc2_10 night the sibling LIGHT-REALISM-1 sweeping-searchlight animation contaminates cross-launch comparison: pose compound_mid shows 6.66% of pixels changed of which 5.19% get BRIGHTER — that is animation, not this gate. The night verdict above is therefore categorical (a named recess that was flat is now visibly darker), and the clean quantitative pass is the day table, whose zero-brighter distribution independently corroborates the mechanism. Also: all six saved mc2_10 night bookmarks are distant overviews (alt 4954-6045) that cannot resolve intra-building occlusion, so four close poses were composed over the tower/compound complex and archived alongside these images. Verify-by-exaggeration was done by stacking the two gates — neither exposes a strength knob (the 0.4 shadow floor is hard-coded) and the shadow-classification debug view is key-toggled only, unreachable headless.

RESIDUAL — this is why neither gate should default ON yet. Alpha-test lattice props self-shadow as solid slabs: the shadow depth pass has no alpha discard, so a chain-link fence writes a solid depth slab into the cascades and then, with RECEIVE ON, samples that slab and darkens uniformly across the whole lattice (image below — it is the single densest diff region on the day poses). Foliage is protected from this by setRecipeNoShadow; fences and railings are not foliage and are not excluded. The clean fix needs a distinct GBuffer1.a class for alpha-test props so they can be excluded from receive — that edits the render-contract mask encoding shared with shadow_screen.frag, too wide to land unverified, so it is logged as follow-up PROP-ALPHA-SHADOW-CLASS-1 rather than guessed at here. ⚠ REVIEW-LANES-LOG-2 CORRECTION — prop self-shadow CANNOT fix the building-face complaint, and MC2_SSAO is broken rather than merely off. Three corrections to this section. (1) A face turned away from the sun already has ndl = 0; a shadow term multiplying zero changes nothing, so MC2_PROP_SHADOW_RECEIVE is architecturally incapable of addressing it — measured, it moves 0.005-0.183% of pixels and only on props like aircraft. (2) The follow-up premise that base_light was the culprit is falsified: a gate built on it was byte-identical at strength 1.0, which multiplies the seed by zero — base_light is effectively ZERO on these props, day and night. The term that actually lights them is ambientTerm, the orientation-free per-actor object-light ambient; that is the real cure site. (3) MC2_SSAO is latent-broken, not off: the AO buffer is white (mean 254.99/255) because aoRadius_ is 3.0 world units against a 42.67 wu map cell — 2% of one cell — and there is no blur pass at all, only a 4-tap box over ±0.5 of a half-res texel, which cannot denoise a 16-sample stochastic kernel. Raising the radius alone therefore trades no-occlusion for visible dither. The 20-60× coverage figure quoted above should not be relied on. blocks.html: Root cause. The min-screen-size clamp added by f412423e was max(1.0, kLbMinNdc / sil) with no upper bound. sil falls off as 1/distance, so k grew without limit and pinned every fixture to a constant hard-edged bright block at every camera distance. Holding a constant screen size was the clamp's literal intent — correct at playable RTS range, which is what made the lights visible at grazing angles — but past that range several hundred regularly-spaced fixtures simply never shrink. Regular spacing + constant size = the dashes. A secondary error compounded it ~1.5x: kLbRefRadius was the authored top-cap radius (0.8), but the rigid billboard maps local Z (the 2.85-unit post axis) onto toCam, so the post foreshortens and the viewer actually sees the local XY cross-section (runwaylight.ase extents 2.015 x 2.326, radius ~1.2). The clamp was sizing against a feature that is never on screen.

Fix. clamp(kLbMinNdc/sil, 1.0, kLbMaxScale) with kLbMaxScale = 2.5 and the corrected reference radius — the legitimate win survives (fixtures still rasterise at playable range) but they resume normal 1/distance shrink and go sub-pixel at overview on their own. Plus the gate is now default-OFF so stock is what ships.

Measured (changed px, |d|>8, BEFORE vs opt-in): overview 549 px in a 136 x 13 horizontal band, 95% of them darker, max delta 240 — that band is the streak. The user's ruling: "do 3, in the index.html — also ... by all concrete I mean only the actual concrete ... obviously runways, roads, other overlays etc. are their own layer and are currently handled by the shader." Two arms are built, both default OFF, and presented here to choose from. Neither is recommended by the lane — the frames are the decision.

ARM A MC2_CEMENT_CONCRETE_TONE=1 — each concrete cell keeps its own art; only its base tone is pulled onto one reference. ARM B MC2_CEMENT_CONCRETE_CANON=1 — every plain-concrete tile samples one canonical cell, so concrete cannot change colour tile to tile at all. Both act only on cells passing an explicit is-this-actually-concrete test (near-neutral chroma ≤ 0.20, band luminance within [0.72,1.32] of the family centre).

SCOPE QUESTION ANSWERED — markings do NOT live in the concrete cells. This is what blocked the previous lane, and the ruling is confirmed twice over. From source: the solid-cement map g_cementLayerIndexBySlot that ARM B repoints is built only from slots where isCement && !isAlpha; alpha cells are explicitly skipped when it is filled, and TileIsRoadArt() says it outright — a slot present in that map is "solid cement, not road". Runway and road art arrives either as an &Overlays id (its own sampler and blend, u_overlaySidecar / terrain_overlay.frag) or as a cement-alpha transition cell, which is appended past the solid range both arms operate on. From measurement: the cement atlas was dumped (new MC2_CEMENT_ATLAS_DUMP diagnostic) and inspected — on mc2_24, not one of the 110 solid cells has a single texel more than 45 luma above its band mean (largest excursion ~11). There is no painted marking art in solid concrete cells to erase. The census reports family_marked=0; a map that does pack paint into a solid cell is detected (>2% of texels >60 luma above band) and excluded from ARM B by index.

MEASURED — and it reframes the problem. Dumping the atlas showed cross-cell base tone is far more uniform than assumed: on mc2_24 the median cell sits at L=146.3 with p05–p95 = 133–148. What actually varies is inside the cells — 78 of 110 cells carry a large dark region, 36–52% of the tile at L≈60 against concrete at L≈147. That in-cell dark art, not cross-cell tone, is the dominant reason concrete reads as changing colour here. It is why ARM B (which replaces the whole cell) moves ~11–15 luma while ARM A (which only rescales base tone) moves ~1–2.

HONEST CAVEAT ON ARM A — read before grading. On mc2_24 ARM A's census line is family=110 adjusted=96 ref_rgb=149.0,146.4,138.4, which is numerically identical to the census of the gate already rejected (MC2_CEMENT_TONE_MATCH, "after is WAY worse"). It differs only where a map packs genuinely non-concrete cement cells. If mc2_24 is the reference, expect to reject ARM A again — the lane will not claim otherwise.

blocks.html: ARM C — what the “dark regions” actually are

A correction to this section, from measurement. The two arms above were built on the premise that solid concrete cells carry no road or marking art — stated in this pack as “markings do NOT live in the concrete cells”, and supported by a test that found no texel more than 45 luma above its cell band. That test looked only at the bright side. The large dark region it then found in 78 of 110 mc2_24 cells was recorded as “authored material (joints, tarmac, shadowed detail)”.

Dumping the atlas and rendering it shows what it is: a baked asphalt road tileset — straights, curves, T-junctions, crossroads with crosswalk stripes, end caps and a multi-lane highway-with-guardrail piece, painted onto a concrete background. Asphalt is dark, which is precisely why the bright-side test could not see it.

blocks.html:
The reframe this forces — there is no concrete tone problem. Measured with the road texels excluded, the concrete background is already one colour on every map: mc2_24 144.7–149.5 (spread 4.7 luma, std 0.89), mc2_05 3.2, mc2_03 2.4, mc2_10 2.0. mc2_23 and mc2_01 show a ~43-luma span driven entirely by two and one cells, and those cells are wide highway pieces — not concrete.

What makes concrete “magically become a different color” inside a cell is a road: background L≈147 against asphalt L≈82, a ~65-luma hard-edged step. That is exactly the class you scoped out — “obviously runways, roads, other overlays etc. are their own layer and are currently handled by the shader.” True for the &Overlays class. Not true for this one: it is baked into the terrain texture catalog, so TileIsRoadArt() reports “solid cement, not road” and every concrete lever treats a road as concrete.
What ARM C does

ARM C MC2_CEMENT_ROAD_ART_DETECT=1 — detect the baked road art and exclude those cells from every concrete treatment (ARM A's tone pass, ARM B's remap, and the choice of canonical cell). Each cell is split against its own [P60,P95] upper mode — the concrete background — rather than the whole-cell band mean, which on a road-heavy cell is dragged down by the road and hides it. A cell with more than 5% of its texels more than 40 luma below that background is flagged as carrying road art.

ARM C on its own changes no pixels. It writes nothing to the atlas and nothing to the slot→layer map; it only changes which cells ARM A and ARM B are allowed to touch. Its purpose is to make the concrete arms obey your own scope ruling.

What ARM C prevents, measured in-engine. Without it, ARM B repoints 90–100% of the road-carrying cells at its canonical cell — and on 5 of the 6 maps that canonical cell is itself a road tile. On mc2_24 the engine logs canon_cell=10 canon_road_frac=0.312 remapped=109 kept_road=0: ARM B erases every junction, curve and end cap and stamps one straight road segment across every plain concrete tile on the map. With ARM C the same map logs canon_cell=0 canon_road_frac=0.000 remapped=31 kept_road=78 — only the genuinely plain cells are collapsed, and the road network survives intact.

The design claim “concrete and pavement do not move at all” is true for concrete, false for pavement. GATE-DEFAULT-TRUTH-1 does not catch it: it compares a gate’s own registry default to its own reader, and this is gate A’s default asserted inside gate B’s prose. gate_default_agreement PASSES in the run measured for this page. This is the sentence to re-check first if anything moves again.
20a. Your four complaints — honest status
One row per complaint. “Delivered” means the code is in the default build, not that anyone has seen it work. Where a cure ships unverified that is said in the same cell, not in a footnote.

rows.html:
1. Concrete tone & transition tiles
“the transition tiles should just use the same concrete texture”

Root cause found and cured. Eleven earlier lanes attacked the cement atlas and none of them could move it, because the defect was never in the atlas. The overlay layer and the terrain chunk layer disagree on four terms over one physical surface, and the missed one is fog: terrain_overlay.frag carries its own in-shader distance fog toward (0.58,0.65,0.75) clamped at 0.70, terrain_lod_chunk.frag has none, and both layers then receive the shared screen-space edge_fog/fog_oob. The overlay is double-fogged, so the two paths diverge with camera distance. Two pieces of the previous lane's own unexplained data prove it: the seam step grows with distance (runway_ground −4.95 L, runway_mid −16.93 L, runway_overview −14.81 L — only a distance-dependent term can do that), and the overlay pixels are blue-dominant (RenderDoc eid 3678 wrote [0.301,0.3083,0.3623]) which its own warm vec3(0.82,0.80,0.76) tint cannot produce — but the fog colour can.

The cure respects your two rulings. Genuine concrete transition tiles adopt the cement atlas albedo and flat light; tiles carrying authored road or runway art keep their albedo and only get their lighting reconciled — repainting those would be the albedo swap you rejected twice as “WAY worse”. Anything the classifier is unsure about is left entirely alone. The authored marching-squares transition shape is untouched; only the colour inside it moves.

⚠ IT SHIPPED WITH A HOLE, AND THE HOLE WAS THE THING YOU REJECTED TWICE. Two follow-up lanes landed the same day and corrected it three ways. (1) The art guard was wrong twice. The “do not repaint this” mark was first stamped only for 9 of the 17 overlay ids — so a dirt track running onto an apron, or a bridge deck meeting a paved pad, was classified as bare concrete and had its hand-placed art overpainted with plain concrete. Widening it to any overlay id was still not enough: mc2_10's roads and its airbase runway carry no overlay id at all — they are authored as cement-alpha transition art over snow — so they were still being repainted, measured at +46.8 L across 23.0% of the mc2_10 runway frame. That is the albedo swap you rejected twice, arriving through a scoping hole rather than through the gate that owns it. The guard is now the presence of authored art of either kind, and only a cement tile with no authored art at all is repainted. (2) The “identical UV math” claim was not true. The terrain shader insets its atlas sample by half a texel; the adopt path omitted it, so within half a texel of every 128 wu tile border the adopted sample reached into the neighbouring atlas cell — laying a thin wrong-coloured fringe along exactly the borders the change exists to make seamless. Same artifact class as the “weird coloured edge” you reported; it would have traded one edge for another. (3) The killswitch was not clean — it still touched a texture unit when off.

UNVERIFIED — no before/after frame exists. Captures were taken that day, but I checked their manifests: every one measured a binary that does not contain any of these commits. Nothing on disk exercises it. And it knowingly makes one thing worse: its own gate doc records that it widens the separate mc2_03 “terrain outside the pads is near-black” contrast, because concrete becomes more uniformly flat-lit while surrounding terrain keeps mix(0.35,1.20,diffuse) with diffuse clamped at 0.02.

2. Runway colour
“all of the runways should be the same color… like in mc2_01”

Not solved, and the reason is arithmetic rather than effort. At your pose — mc2_10 saved_204937, which is night, not dusk — the apron slabs read mean luma 90.43 and the runway 66.51: a gap of +23.92 L between two surfaces both sitting in the L~66–90 range. Driving the flat-lighting lever MC2_CEMENT_LIT to maximum strength moves the apron down to 84.63 and closes the gap only to +18.12 — 24% of it — and then stalls. The runway value is bit-identical (61.56 / 71.46) across all four arms. That is direct empirical proof the lighting lever cannot reach overlay pavement at all.

The direction even reverses by time of day: on mc2_24 in daylight the same gate widens the concrete-vs-road gap from +16.38 to +17.71, because normalLight = mix(0.35,1.20,diffuse) exceeds 1.0 on well-lit surfaces so cement brightens. A lever whose sign depends on time of day is not a uniformity fix.

What is left is an albedo change — and that is exactly the class of change you have rejected twice. Nobody has designed a third approach.

⚠ AND THE ONE LEVER THAT DID FLIP ON WAS FLIPPED BACK OFF THE SAME DAY. The classification gate MC2_PAVED_OVERLAY_CLASS was promoted to default-ON as “the lever for all of the runways should be the same color” — and then reverted, because a previous lane had already measured that mode at your own night poses and found it made things worse: max delta 20–29/255 and 9.2–21.7% hard-step pixels — “it ADDS hard-edged outlines rather than removing them”. The promotion flipped a gate whose own retraction was already sitting on disk. It is default-OFF again, which is what the top of this page already says.
(The underlying classification finding still stands: at your pose the runway is 100% unclassified — zero cement classification, pure colormap.)

Net for this complaint: nothing shipped, and nothing is queued.

3. Vehicles not on the same lighting path
“that is just wrong… it is the lighting path”

You were right, and here is the mechanism. Every other object class populates its per-object light row via CacheGpuLightData() before drawing — mechs (mech3d.cpp:5614), buildings (bdactor.cpp:3144/:3181/:4821), trees (:6566), generic props (genactor.cpp:1256). GVAppearance called neither that nor the batcher, yet renders unconditionally through the legacy TG_Shape::Render path, which consumes lightData_ (tgl.cpp:3508) with no gather and no eligibility guard. The chain, each link cited to a committed blob: numLights_ zero-inits (tgl.h:339) → addLightDataStructure is pure dedup/append with no back-fill, so the all-zero row is stored verbatim (txmmgr.cpp:1929-1988) → calc_light takes its numLights.x==0 early return and returns vec3(1,1,1), discarding even the per-vertex base_light (lighting.hglsl:232-236) → the fragment shader multiplies by it. Vehicles drew at raw albedo × 1.0 — completely unlit, day and night. Buildings reach that same legacy path only as a fallback they normally never take, so vehicles were the only class actually exercising an ungathered row.

This also settles the old “trucks are just darker textures” thread: the albedo measurement was right (trucksprop.tga masked luminance 85.9 vs a 787-texture corpus median of 86.2 — 49th percentile, dead average) and the albedo theory was wrong. Mechs and buildings get ambient + sun×ndl, which exceeds 1.0 in daylight, so a median-brightness texture at ×1.0 still looks dark parked beside one. RETRACTED in fc43338a.

The follow-up matters. The first commit lit exactly one leaf per vehicle, because CacheGpuLightData() populates only firstShapeNodeLeaf (correct for the batcher, which broadcasts it; wrong for the legacy path, where TG_MultiShape::Render loops every leaf and each submits its own row). ccb713ae gathers for all leaves.

UNVERIFIED — mechanism proven, pixels not. MC2_LIGHT_ROW_CENSUS fires with the gate on and is completely silent with MC2_VEHICLE_LIT_PATH=0 on both missions (mc2_03 day: AMBIENT seen=5000, INFINITE 4998; mc2_10 night: POINT 151385, SPOT 13232, AMBIENT 10601) — so vehicles demonstrably went from no light row to real gathered rows. But at every pose that is byte-stable within a single arm, ON and OFF are byte-identical; and the poses that do differ between arms also drift within a single arm. Earlier “+14.8 / +18.8 luma brighter” readings are RETRACTED — the changed pixels were a turret barrel at a different aim angle and building windows at a different animation phase. Vehicles are movers, so byte-diff A/B is structurally unable to evaluate exactly the objects this changes. A mover-freeze fixture is the prerequisite, and it does not exist. One more gap I measured directly: the 27 A/B manifests on disk carry no binary-provenance field at all and name a worktree commit that precedes ccb713ae — so even the all-leaves follow-up, the half that actually lights the whole vehicle, has no capture attributable to it.

The cause is understood as a class, both previous cures were rejected by you, and the newest proposed cure was falsified before anyone built it. A B-spline-residual design was written to be one-sided-safe (it can only add water, never delete it, so it can fill notches but never shave a seaward tongue). An offline falsification lane ran it over the shipping heightfields — no engine, no build — and returned NO-GO against the design's own decision rule (“abandon if median reach is under ~40 wu”): mc2_17 comes in at 5.1 wu, roughly 1/20th of the threshold and 1/20th of a 128 wu tile riser. The budget C = k·alphaDepth/2 is 5–10 wu, shore slope is 0.12–0.35, so the contour can move ~5–36 wu. “You cannot move a contour 128 wu with a 5 wu budget on a 0.12 slope.”

And a larger result: mc2_17's waterline is not stair-stepped in the shipping heightfield at all. Staircase index 0.260 against an isotropic-curve floor of 0.222 — within noise of a smooth curve. mc2_10 scores 0.737 and is a textbook tile-locked staircase. The mechanism every shoreline design has been written for is on a different map from the complaint.

This is the third shoreline mechanism to die on the same structural point, and the pattern is now named: any knob whose budget is specified in elevation units inherits 1/|grad| and will be weakest on flat shelves — which is exactly where the defect is worst. A cure has to be specified in horizontal distance.

Next lead, untested: terrain LOD decimation at gameplay altitude — if shore blocks render at lodStep>1 the land/water edge would step at 256/512 wu granularity, which would look exactly like the complaint and is invisible to full-resolution heightfield analysis.

blocks.html: 20b. Trees, black quads, sunk turrets

Three defects that were not fixed. One had a false closure removed; two are still uncaused. The useful part of all three is the same discovery: the tests that were supposed to cover them cannot reach them.

rows.html:
A previous session closed this as “CLOSED, NO DEFECT — the silhouettes are baked colormap art from burnInShadows”. That closure is now refuted, not merely unsupported — and it left no artifact on disk anywhere, so there was nothing to re-read.

Refuted at source: burnInShadows (mclib/terrtxm2.cpp:609) builds a height map, ray-marches shadows through that, and modulates the colormap. It never touches an object list, an appearance, a TG_Shape, or any prop or tree structure. It cannot produce a tree-shaped silhouette.
Refuted in the texels. The mission's own object list was parsed out of the shipping archive: 2560 objects — 2088 TREE, 241 terrain objects, 219 buildings, 11 turrets, 1 gate. Every one of the 2088 tree positions was tested for a core-vs-ring darkening against the deployed colormap under all 8 orientations (4 rotations × optional mirror), so no orientation choice could rescue the claim. Every reading is within 1.5σ and inside the spread of the random control points; p(core darker) never exceeds 0.541 — a coin flip. The statistic is strong enough to exclude any silhouette of depth ≥20 luminance on more than ~2.4% of the trees.
A structural backstop makes it moot anyway: the stock burn-in is 1280² over 12800 world units — 10 world units per pixel — and a tree card is 2–4 pixels. A recognisable tree silhouette cannot come from that texture at any resolution in the chain.

The real finding, and it is structural. TreeAppearance::update writes the terrain light sample into slot 1, the AMBIENT light (bdactor.cpp:6924) and then deactivates the sun outright — light->active = false at :6938, restored only at :7054, with the static light bake at :7039 sitting inside that window. GatherLightsParameters skips inactive lights (txmmgr.cpp:2488), so a tree's light row contains one AMBIENT entry and no INFINITE entry at all. The shader's sun scan (static_prop.vert:715-728) therefore never finds one and sunColor stays vec3(0.0), which makes the load-bearing line lit = (seed + ambientTerm) * propDirFactor + sunColor * ndl (:823) carry a term that is identically zero for every tree.
Buildings do the opposite — they write to slot 0 and leave the sun active (bdactor.cpp:3856).
Consequence: MC2_PROP_FOLIAGE_ALPHAFLAG, which only changes how ndl is computed, is a guaranteed no-op for trees on a default launch — it is multiplied by zero.

This is not a port regression. Both lines are present in the first commit of the imported Microsoft source. Trees have always been ambient-only. What changed is the consumer: static_prop.vert has no ambient floor and no protective early return, unlike calc_light, which returns vec3(1) when a row is empty.

Nothing shipped. 03519ea1 is one file, +402 lines of markdown, no code, no gate, no build, no launch. Seven discriminating A/B tests are specified and none were run, because launches are blocked. And the lane says the honest thing: “I never saw the user's frame… the single highest-value next step is asking the user which frame.”

The defect, stated precisely for the first time: on BTurretControl and LiaoTurretGenerator the window and vent panels render as solid pure-black quads (RGB 0,0,0) with a dithered 1-bit-alpha fringe, while the same window bands on LiaoHeavyGateControl, the Barracks and the Quonsets render correctly. So a pose that frames only the latter grades nothing — which is exactly what earlier work did. The previous pose set sat inside the same walled compound but at altitude 650, where it framed the perimeter wall and the Quonset row and the defect is simply not in shot.

One cause is ruled out: the far-backdrop path is not it — across six poses there were no black quads to fix. (Those six poses were the wrong frame, which is itself the finding.)
Nothing is ruled in. UNCAUSED.

Uncaused, and worse — barely described. The defect survives on disk as a two-word phrase in a session ledger and a single pose-coverage tag (turret_ground_seating). There is no prose anywhere saying what “sunk” means concretely — how far, which turrets, or a screenshot. UNVERIFIED as a defect description, not just as a fix.
A related live observation was recorded earlier and left open: turret animation is gated at bdactor.cpp:3326, and frozen turrets were seen at a night pose but never reproduced.

blocks.html: ⚠ THE KEY INSIGHT, and it applies to both of the uncaused defects. The live lead is BldgAppearance::setGesture (mclib/bdactor.cpp:1829-1848): an idle building that is registered as a static prop has its static registration invalidated on its first gesture, because the GPU registry is holding a stale static-pose recipe. It fires at most once per building, ever — bdAnimationState never returns to idle, there is no reset path. No test that has ever run reaches that line. The only entry point is Building::updateAnimations(), whose ~17 gesture calls all sit inside gameplay state switches — sensor-tower contact counts, gate open/close cycles, damage and destruction. The smoke tier is five stock missions, 30 seconds each, idle fly-throughs: no AI engagement, no weapon fire, no gate traversal, so no building ever leaves the idle state and the counter stays zero. This was designed in and disclosed from the start — the 2026-06-03 implementation plan says the path would be “code-reviewed but not runtime-exercised” and told reviewers not to block on it. A fixture that fires a building gesture is the prerequisite for testing this defect class at all. It does not exist.

Two honesty notes on the evidence behind the paragraph above. (1) Seventeen capture arms were run against the airfield (scratch/mc203air/, 6 poses each at 4K) and produced no written verdict of any kind — no status document exists for that lane in any worktree. (2) The anim-gate A/B arm was run without its own instrument switched on: the [ANIM_GATE v1] counter is emitted through a diagnostic macro that is invisible unless a verbosity variable is set, and that variable is in no arm’s environment. Grepping all seventeen capture logs for it returns zero hits. So “the path was never exercised” rests on reading the source, not on a measured zero. Stated as UNVERIFIED rather than asserted.

blocks.html: 20i. Root causes that MOVED — corrections to §20a and §20b

Four investigations changed their answer after §20a/§20b were written. Three of them killed a mechanism the whole session had been reasoning from. None of the four produced a fix, and that is the point: the value here is that four wrong roads are now closed, cheaply, without a launch. Nothing in this sub-section is a delivered change.

rows.html: Two unrelated defects, cause unknown, with a LOD-swap mechanism cited as the likely path for both.

A SINGLE candidate root cause now covers both. A static prop recipe is a frozen snapshot that is not invalidated when a building becomes ineligible via a state-to-state gesture, flash or activity — so a live recipe holds a stale pose. Black outlines: the shadow-caster feed walks the full registry, visibility- and eligibility-independent, and is DEFAULT-ON — so an animating building casts a shadow from its mission-load pose. Sunk turrets: turrets have no ground-snap at all, and the recipe bakes the raw .ase rest pose pre-snap.

OPEN — NOT CONFIRMED. These are ranked hypotheses with default-ON reachability proven at source, not a diagnosis. Settled by decision 11: list the buildings on mc2_03, then a one-frame shadow-caster A/B.
Building LOD swaps were the leading explanation for prop pop and were reasoned from repeatedly.
IT CANNOT FIRE. Building LOD is pinned to 0. Every chain of reasoning that routed through it is void.

RETRACTED. The memory file asserting the mechanism is stale and should not be trusted until corrected. Worth noting how this survived so long: it was in a memory file, and memory files are not covered by any contract.
The one-sided-safe B-spline was the designed cure; mc2_17 and mc2_10 were the same tile-locked defect.

The B-spline was FALSIFIED OFFLINE before it was built: it moves the waterline 5.1 wu against the ~100 wu required. mc2_17 is NOT tile-locked (staircase index 0.260 vs a 0.222 floor); mc2_10 IS (0.737). Different defects. The real mc2_17 mechanism is the drape cap handing the edge to the depth test at 128 wu on 66.7% of the waterline.

RETRACTED · OPEN
A general principle now kills a whole FAMILY of cures: anything budgeted in elevation units inherits 1/|grad| and is weakest exactly where the defect is worst. Blocked on decision 1 (displacement or faceting?).
Tree silhouettes were suspected to be baked into the art.
Proven NOT baked art — 2,088 positions measured under all 8 orientations. The real finding: trees carry no directional light at all, so sunColor * ndl is identically zero.

FALSE LEAD CLOSED · OPEN
A real, specific, mechanism-level cause now exists with no cure attached. This is the same shape as the vehicle defect (numLights==0 → vec3(1,1,1)) that VEHICLE-LIGHTING-PATH-1 addressed — which makes it a strong candidate for the same treatment, and a strong candidate to have the same untested night direction.

blocks.html:
Two mechanical blocks are now live and tested, and both exist because a written rule was violated repeatedly. (1) Game launches are hard-blocked by a PreToolUse hook. You reported five separate times that agent launches steal your mouse, keyboard and focus. Every prompt-level rule was violated anyway, so the block is now mechanical. It is not being worked around — this update was written entirely from source, git, and offline file inspection, and the hook fired once during it (on a command that merely named the binary to read its timestamp) and was obeyed. (2) git add -A / git add . / git commit -a are blocked, because several lanes share worktrees and a sweep stages other lanes’ work. That happened twice.

The honest cost of block (1), stated plainly: it is now the binding constraint on the project. Every pixel-changing change on this page is UNVERIFIED because of it, and no amount of further source reading will change that — the remaining questions are questions about pixels. That is what decision 11 is asking you to unblock, once, supervised.

What this update did NOT do — stated so it is not mistaken for coverage. Nothing was built and nothing was launched. Every pixel statement in §20 is derived from shader and C++ source. No luma number on this page was measured by anyone this session. A clean build of the tip was not attempted: the merge audit deliberately did not stash, because three lanes’ uncommitted work is sitting in the canonical worktree and stashing it is the exact hazard being audited. So “no line was dropped” is proven; “the merged tree compiles” is not. The contract audit injected against 6 of 98 rows and did a structural census of the rest — the older checks are unexamined, and the identifier-in-a-comment defect appearing three times suggests a systematic comment-stripping audit of all 73 tree-inspecting checks would pay. Binary fingerprinting covered engine binaries only; editor and tool executables were not checked, and three mod installs carry no fingerprint banner at all. Finally, a build from the canonical worktree right now would be stamped BUILT-FROM-DIRTY-TREE and its manifest src_commit suffixed -dirty — though the dirty edits themselves add no default pixel change (two are comment-only; the rest are guarded by an env var that is unset).
